clue.text: Reserved arena and sportingly fought

parts.note: a ring is an arena for boxing or the circus
fenced, as in the sport of fencing with foils or sabres

explanation.surface: A sports ground set aside for a duel fought in good spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Money that is ring-fenced is earmarked or protected for one purpose only, so it is set aside.

clue.text: Sporting trial includes children's game: come on, young lady!

indicators.note: includes means the anagrammed letters hold the game's letters inside them
sporting here means playing about, so the letters of trial are rearranged

parts.note: tag is the playground chasing game

explanation.surface: A sports trial featuring a playground game, with an encouraging shout to a girl taking part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' looks like it describes the trial, but it is the signal to shuffle; the game sits inside the shuffled letters, near the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is a cheer of encouragement or praise aimed at a girl or woman, like 'well done, girl!'

clue.text: Interfere in award to be announced

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so the word for award is taken by its sound

parts.note: a medal is an award

explanation.surface: Someone meddling in the decision over a prize that is yet to be made public.
explanation.definitionFit: To meddle is to poke one's nose into other people's affairs, a synonym of interfere.

clue.text: Appear depressed, but work through debilitating condition

indicators.note: through means the word for work runs through the middle of the condition

parts.note: ME is myalgic encephalomyelitis, chronic fatigue syndrome
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Someone looking down but still working despite a chronic illness.
explanation.walkthrough: ME is the name used in Britain for chronic fatigue syndrome.
explanation.definitionFit: To mope is to sulk listlessly and look miserable, which is appearing low in spirits.

clue.text: Rely on this unwritten promise? Goodness!

definitions.meaning: first sense: a spoken pledge, trusting what someone has said
second sense: an old-fashioned exclamation of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the phrase is a guarantee given by voice alone, with nothing on paper; as a phrase it is mild astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a dated exclamation of surprise, and literally means trusting someone's spoken assurance.

clue.text: Lengthen pamphlet after person making regular cuts

indicators.note: after means the pamphlet word comes behind the word for the person

parts.note: a pro, a professional, takes a regular cut or fee from the work done
a tract is a short religious or political pamphlet

explanation.surface: Someone who edits regularly stretching out a leaflet instead of trimming it.
explanation.walkthrough: The cutting in the surface suggests an editor; the job here is simply a professional, PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: To protract is to draw out or prolong something in time, a synonym of extend.

clue.text: Hi there, Richard: Hamlet knew him

parts.note: yo is a slangy greeting
Rick is a short form of the name Richard

explanation.surface: A casual greeting to a man called Richard, who the Prince of Denmark once knew.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes Hamlet's line over a skull: 'Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio.'
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's play the prince recognises the skull of the late court jester he knew as a child.

clue.text: Quick look as dog is heard

indicators.note: is heard means the dog's name is taken by how it sounds

parts.note: a peke is a Pekinese, a small Chinese breed

explanation.surface: A brief glance at a dog that can be heard barking.
explanation.definitionFit: A peek is a brief, often furtive glance, a quick look.

clue.text: Having toilet break, quietly kept in touch

parts.note: someone taking a toilet break is in the loo
p is piano, the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Someone stepping out to the lavatory but still discreetly informed of what's going on.
explanation.walkthrough: Loo is everyday British for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the loop is an idiom for being informed and part of the communications on a matter.

clue.text: Edge past river; this one?

indicators.note: past means the word for edge comes beyond, after the river letter

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river
to hone is to sharpen, to put an edge on

explanation.surface: Sneaking along the bank of a waterway, asking which river this is.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the answer is a river of the kind it describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhône is a major river flowing from Switzerland through France to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Nob's name entered in fifth rank

definitions.note: Nob's reads as 'Nob is', and the definition is the noun Nob

indicators.note: entered in means the abbreviation for name goes inside the other letters

parts.note: a grade is a rank or level
E is the fifth letter, so grade E is the fifth rank

explanation.surface: A posh person's name being put down in a low category.
explanation.walkthrough: Nob is British slang for a toff, a person of high rank; the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandee is a nobleman or a person of high social standing, as a nob is.

clue.text: Be fussy in dealing with infestation

definitions.meaning: first sense: to criticise petty details
second sense: literally picking nits, louse eggs, from hair

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the word literally: combing out nits.
explanation.definitionFit: To nitpick is to find fault over trivial matters; literally it means removing lice eggs one by one.

clue.text: French boy using English measure

parts.note: an imperial measure of distance, 1,760 yards

explanation.surface: A French lad sticking to imperial units of length.
explanation.definitionFit: Émile is a French boy's name, famously the title of Rousseau's treatise on education.

clue.text: Would-be regicide, chap goes two ways in speech

parts.note: a guy is a chap

indicators.note: in speech means the word is taken as said rather than as spelt

parts.note: a road that forks goes off two ways

explanation.surface: A man who would kill a king, talking out of both sides of his mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Guy Fawkes tried to blow up King James I in the 1605 Gunpowder Plot; in non-rhotic British speech FORKS and FAWKES sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: He plotted to kill the king but failed, so he was an attempted king-killer.

clue.text: In a match, goalie who has grouse to nurse

parts.note: a game is a match
a keeper is a goalkeeper

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper in a match nursing a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like a grumble, but it is the game bird; on British shooting estates a gamekeeper rears grouse for shoots.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamekeeper is employed to protect and rear game birds on an estate for shooting.

clue.text: Tacitly agreed to break heartless spy — no difficulty

indicators.note: to break means the agreed word splits the shortened spy word apart
heartless means the middle letter of spy is removed, leaving its two ends

parts.note: taken as written
implicit means understood without being stated

explanation.surface: An unspoken pact lets a ruthless agent be cracked without trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' leaves only the outside letters of the agent, and 'to break' wedges the agreement word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Simplicity is the quality of being easy, free of complication or difficulty.

clue.text: Old Mac from croft developed novel smallholding

indicators.note: developed means the letters are worked up into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Old MacDonald's croft built up into a small farm.
explanation.walkthrough: A croft is a small Scottish farm; 'Old Mac' recalls Old MacDonald who had a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Stella Gibbons's comic novel takes its title from the run-down Sussex farm where it is set.

clue.text: No participant in the betting, but one rakes it in

definitions.text: No participant in the betting, but one rakes it in

parts.words: No participant in the betting, but one rakes it in
parts.note: the casino employee does not bet but gathers in the chips with a rake

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rakes it in' sounds like getting rich; literally the casino worker drags the chips across the table with a little rake.
explanation.definitionFit: A croupier runs a gaming table in a casino, collecting and paying out stakes without gambling.

clue.text: Bad feeling, as I'm taken in by a mate

indicators.note: taken in by means the letters of I'm are put inside the other words

parts.note: a crony is a close friend, a mate

explanation.surface: Resentment because a friend has fooled the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrimony is bitterness or ill will in speech or manner, a kind of bad feeling.

clue.text: No longer a priest? Fabulous — was really good!

parts.note: def is slang for excellent, fabulous
rocked is slang for was excellent

explanation.surface: An ex-priest reviewing a great gig in slang.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as by example: unfrocking is one way to stop being a priest.
explanation.definitionFit: A defrocked priest has been stripped of holy orders for misconduct, so is a priest no more.

clue.text: Idle autumn: nothing before onset of winter

parts.note: fall is the American word for autumn
O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: onset of means only the opening letter of winter is used

explanation.surface: An unproductive autumn with nothing doing before the cold sets in.
explanation.definitionFit: Fallow land is left unplanted for a season, so it lies unused and inactive.

clue.text: Threat of proper illumination?

indicators.note: of means the answer is taken from within the following words

explanation.surface: A question about the danger posed by lighting done properly.
explanation.definitionFit: A peril is a serious danger, something that threatens harm.

clue.text: Drinking beer, work steadily but dimly

indicators.note: drinking means the word for work steadily takes in the beer

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it steadily
ale is a beer

explanation.surface: Someone nursing a pint but working away with little brightness.
explanation.definitionFit: Shining palely means giving a weak, faint light, so not brightly.

clue.text: Initially ready to please, suffering setback

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of ready is used
suffering means the letters of please are in a bad way, so rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone eager to please at first, then going downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffering setback' reads as one phrase, but 'suffering' is the anagram signal and only 'setback' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A relapse is a return to illness or bad ways after improvement, a reversal of progress.

clue.text: Cut of meat for shelf

definitions.meaning: first sense: a ... of lamb, a joint with ribs
second sense: a framework for holding things

explanation.definitionFit: A rack of lamb is a rib joint, and a rack is also a frame or set of shelves for storage.

clue.text: Hate speech perhaps gets Mike arrested by police with violence

indicators.note: arrested by means the letter is held inside the rearranged letters
with violence means the letters of police are roughly rearranged

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man called Mike detained by heavy-handed officers over a hateful speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'police' looks like the arresting party in the surface, but its letters are the anagram fodder that holds Mike.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemic is a strongly worded attack on someone's views; hate speech is one extreme example.

clue.text: One of two bound for power

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: One of a pair heading towards authority.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby, a team's two props bind on to the hooker in the scrum front row.
explanation.definitionFit: A prop is one of the two front-row forwards in a rugby scrum, who are bound together.

clue.text: Preferred a thing from Paris

definitions.meaning: first sense: picked, selected over others
second sense: the French word for a thing

explanation.definitionFit: Chose is the past tense of choose, selected; in French une chose is a thing.

clue.text: One dumped on old aircraft — time to see another world

parts.note: an ex is a former partner, one who has been dumped
a plane is an aircraft

explanation.surface: A jilted lover flying off in an ancient aeroplane in search of a new life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' looks like a single letter, but 'One dumped' together is an ex.
explanation.definitionFit: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun, a world beyond our solar system.
